n: In this lesson we study destructive poisons. The lesson plan has six parts. First, the general characterisation: composition, mechanism and cumulation. Then mercury: corrosive sublimate and organic compounds. The third part is lead: salts and tetraethyl lead. The fourth is thallium: signs and the forensic situation. The fifth is arsenic: two forms, post-mortem signs and cumulation. Finally, diagnosis: history, clinical picture and laboratory.

Briefly on the first section. Destructive poisons are heavy metals and arsenic. These substances are mercury, lead, thallium and arsenic. Their action is based on binding the sulphydryl groups of enzymes. An important feature is cumulation, that is, accumulation in the body. Nowadays such poisoning is rare and is mainly observed in occupational activity.

t: Place in the classification: resorptive poisons
n: Let us look at the place in the classification. Resorptive poisons are divided into three groups. The destructive group includes mercury, lead, zinc, arsenic and phosphorus; in them tissue structure is disrupted. Haemotropic, that is, blood poisons are divided into haemoglobinotropic, haemolytic and other blood poisons. Functional poisons act on the central nervous system or the peripheral nervous system. Today we will consider the destructive group.

The mechanism of resorptive action proceeds in sequence. First the poison is absorbed into the blood. Then the sulphydryl groups are bound. As a result enzymes are inactivated. Finally metabolism and organ function are disturbed. Remember: the basis of action of this group is the binding of sulphydryl groups.

Most destructive poisons accumulate in the body; this is cumulation. As to present-day occurrence: they are rarely encountered in forensic practice. The main link is with occupational activity. Mushrooms accumulate heavy metals. In a mushroom beside a busy road, hundreds of times more accumulates than in one from the ground.

The second section: mercury, in brief. Pure mercury taken by mouth does not poison, because it does not dissolve. The dangerous states are finely dispersed and vapour, because they enter by inhalation. An inorganic example is mercury dichloride, that is, corrosive sublimate. Organic compounds include granosan and mercuzan. Mercury is preserved for a long time in the body: it is detected even after decades.

The state of mercury determines the danger. The pure metal taken by mouth does not dissolve and does not poison. In a finely dispersed state it is absorbed by inhalation, and in vapour form it causes severe poisoning. Its compounds are of greater forensic importance. Inorganic compounds include corrosive sublimate, calomel and mercury cyanide. Examples of organic compounds are granosan and mercuzan.

Corrosive sublimate dissolves well in water and is used as an antiseptic. It is regarded as a strong protoplasmic poison. The mechanism is this: the sublimate acts on tissue proteins, mercury albuminates form, and as a result protein function in metabolism is disturbed. That is, the poison combines with proteins and upsets their work.

t: Corrosive sublimate: clinical picture and cause of death
n: The clinical picture of corrosive sublimate and the cause of death. Poisoning usually lasts up to a week. There is a burn of the mouth, oesophagus and stomach, a metallic taste and severe pain. Vomit contains blood, and sometimes diarrhoea is also observed. In the kidneys oliguria develops, then anuria. In the heart and nervous system there are weakening, convulsions and loss of consciousness. The cause of death is acute renal failure.

t: Corrosive sublimate: the body, mouth and intestine
n: In the body after sublimate poisoning, in rapid death there is inflammation at the site of contact. Inflammation, sometimes necrosis, is found in the oesophagus and stomach. In the oral cavity, mercurial stomatitis and gingivitis develop. A dirty-grey border appears at the gum margin. In the large intestine diphtheritic inflammation is observed; this is called sublimate dysentery.

In later death, changes are in the organs that excrete the poison. In the macroscopic appearance of the sublimate kidney, the kidney is enlarged and the capsule tense. The cortex is thickened and the pyramids are dark cherry in colour. Microscopically, toxic necronephrosis is identified. In other organs degeneration and necrobiotic changes occur.

Poisoning with calomel and mercury cyanide is relatively rare. Calomel, that is, mercury chloride, is poorly soluble in water. It was formerly used as a laxative. It poisons when accumulated in the intestine in a large dose. Mercury cyanide reacts with the hydrochloric acid of the stomach, and hydrocyanic acid is formed. Therefore poisoning develops.

Remember the lethal doses given in the textbook. For corrosive sublimate 0.1–0.3 g. For calomel 2.0–3.0 g. For mercury cyanide 0.2–1.0 g. For granosan 0.2–0.4 g. As you see, the lethal dose of calomel is considerably larger than the others.

Organic mercury compounds are used in agriculture as insectofungicides. The route of poisoning is consumption of the treated product. As an example, flour from grain treated with granosan is cited. Poisoning usually runs a chronic course. The poison enters in small amounts and accumulates in the body.

We compare inorganic and organic mercury. With inorganic mercury the kidney and large intestine are clearly damaged, with organic mercury less so. Stomatitis develops with inorganic mercury and does not develop with organic. The neurotoxic effect is less with inorganic and stronger with organic. Clinically, with inorganic mercury gastrointestinal and renal signs predominate, with organic toxic encephalopathy.

t: Organic mercury: stages of the course
n: The course of organic mercury is by stages. The first stage is the latent period: there are no signs for up to several months. The second is general signs: weakness, insomnia, weight loss. The third is disturbance of systems: nervous, cardiac and intestinal. The fourth is the chronic period: tremor, and also disturbance of handwriting, speech and gait. Clinical signs begin after several months.

Signs of chronic mercury poisoning. There is fine tremor of the fingers, eyelids and tongue. Handwriting, gait and speech change. In emotional state the patient is irritable, tearful and timid. In severe cases the psyche changes. Before death, body temperature rises. That is, change of the nervous system and psyche is the main sign.

t: Chronic mercury: examination of the body
n: Examination of the body in chronic mercury poisoning. Mercury accumulates in the brain, bone and kidney. The body is emaciated and the blood thick. In the brain and soft meninges there are oedema and congestion. Small haemorrhages occur on serous membranes and the intestinal mucosa. Fatty degeneration and toxic hepatitis are found in the liver, and toxic necronephrosis in the kidneys.

The third section: lead, in brief. Lead salts are chloride, nitrate, acetate. The organic compound is tetraethyl lead. It acts on enzymes and proteins. The main damage is in the central and peripheral nerves, and also anaemia. Poisoning occurs occupationally or through an accident.

With lead, albuminates form and enzymes are inactivated. Inorganic salts are water-soluble: chloride, nitrate, acetate. They enter mainly by mouth and are eliminated through the intestine, kidneys and salivary glands. Tetraethyl lead was an antiknock agent in leaded petrol and its use is now prohibited. It enters through skin, mouth and respiratory tract.

Let us look at the difference between lead and mercury. The intestine and kidney are more affected in mercury and less so in lead. The central and peripheral nerves are damaged less in mercury and more seriously in lead. Characteristic of mercury are stomatitis and nephrosis, of lead delirium, convulsions and paraesthesia. In addition: with mercury oliguria and anuria, with lead paralysis and anaemia.

The mechanism of tetraethyl lead. In the brain the enzymes pyruvate dehydrogenase and cholinesterase are blocked. As a result pyruvate and acetylcholine accumulate. After a short latent period hypotonia, bradycardia and psychosis appear. That is, the poison acts first of all on brain enzymes.

The clinical picture of tetraethyl lead begins after a latent period. At the start there are a fall in temperature and hypotonia. Vegetative signs: bradycardia, sweating and salivation. In the psyche hallucinations and acute psychosis are observed. In psychomotor state there is agitation or catatonic stupor. Later convulsions and coma develop.

The fourth section: thallium, in brief. Thallium salts resemble table salt. More often the cause of poisoning is an accident. The forensic situation is that thallium has also been used for homicide. Characteristic signs: gastroenteritis, ataxia and alopecia. In polyneuropathy there is severe pain. In diagnosis, the result of toxicological examination is decisive.

The clinical signs of thallium appear in several systems. In the gastrointestinal tract there are signs of gastroenteritis. In coordination of movement, ataxia is observed. The skin undergoes trophic changes. Hair falls out; this is alopecia. In the peripheral nerve, polyneuropathy and severe pain appear.

The fifth section: arsenic, in brief. All arsenic compounds are poisonous, the trivalent more strongly. Paris green and arsenites occur. Pure arsenic does not dissolve and is not poisonous. Elimination is very slow, mainly through the kidneys. The lethal dose is 0.1–0.2 g. The forms of poisoning are gastrointestinal and paralytic.

Use and occurrence of arsenic. Nowadays arsenic compounds are used very rarely. In agriculture they were used against insects and rodents. Preparations: Paris green, sodium and calcium arsenite. A present-day cause is environmental pollution. Sometimes it is used for suicide. In history, it was often used for homicide.

The toxicity of arsenic depends on valency. Pure arsenic does not dissolve in water or fat, and therefore is not poisonous. If it is oxidised in air, a poisonous compound forms. All its compounds are poisonous. Trivalent ones are more poisonous than pentavalent ones.

The mechanism of action of arsenic. At the site of contact there is inflammation, and with prolonged contact necrosis. In the enzyme system sulphydryl groups are blocked and metabolism is disturbed. In the vessels, capillaries dilate paralytically. As a result blood pressure falls sharply and collapse develops. In resorptive action the brain and vessels are damaged.

Arsenic is eliminated from the body very slowly. The lethal dose is 0.1–0.2 g. The main route of elimination is the kidney. A lesser route is the intestinal mucosa. Additional routes are sweat, saliva and bile. Because of slow elimination, the poison stays in the body for a long time.

In acute arsenic poisoning two forms are distinguished. In the gastrointestinal form the poison is taken by mouth, with vomiting and cholera-like diarrhoea and dehydration; death occurs on day 1–2. In the paralytic form a large amount is introduced by mouth or parenterally, signs of toxic encephalopathy appear, digestive signs are weak or absent, and death occurs in the first hours.

The clinical picture of the gastrointestinal form. In the first hour a metallic taste appears in the mouth. There are burning and severe pain in the mouth and abdomen. Incessant vomiting is observed. After a while diarrhoea, as in cholera. In the general state dehydration and hepatorenal disturbance develop. Severe signs: the voice becomes hoarse, cyanosis and convulsions.

The clinical picture of the paralytic form. Signs of toxic encephalopathy are prominent. At the start headache and dizziness are felt. Then disturbance of consciousness: delirium and loss of consciousness. In a short time coma and convulsions appear. Finally, paralysis of the respiratory and cardiac centres leads to death.

In chronic arsenic poisoning the signs develop slowly and in many systems. In the digestive system there is dyspepsia. In the nervous system, signs of polyneuropathy are observed. Body weight falls. Hair falls out. Transverse white bands appear on the nails.

In the gastrointestinal form, examination of the body shows dehydration and intestinal inflammation. The blood is thickened. In the gastrointestinal mucosa there is serous-fibrinous-haemorrhagic inflammation. In the mucosa, oedema, haemorrhage, necrosis and erosions occur. In the small intestine there is a liquid mass and flakes. In the serosa and abdominal cavity a viscous fibrinous-haemorrhagic exudate is found.

In the paralytic form morphological changes are minimal. In the meninges of the brain there are marked oedema and congestion. In the brain and parenchymatous organs there are many small haemorrhages. Streaky haemorrhages are found in the endocardium of the left ventricle. In the gastrointestinal mucosa there are oedema, small haemorrhages and catarrhal signs.

Cumulation of arsenic is important for forensic examination: arsenic is preserved in the body for years. It accumulates in internal organs and bone, that is, in the liver and bones. It also accumulates in skin appendages: skin, hair and nails. For this reason examination is possible even after a long time.

Let us consider what diagnosis relies on. The first is history, which is gathered thoroughly. The second is the set of clinical and morphological changes. The third is toxicological examination: blood, urine, vomit and gastric lavage fluid. Remember: toxicological results are decisive.

The first teaching case: protracted poisoning. This is a hypothetical case, not a real examination. Given: flour from grain treated with granosan was consumed, and for several months there were no signs. Then weakness, insomnia and a metallic taste appeared, followed by ataxia, visual disturbance and tremor. Questions: to which type of poisoning does it correspond, is stomatitis expected, and what is the kidney damage?

The answer to the first case: the set of signs corresponds to organic mercury. The most suitable type is the organic mercury compound, chronic. The reason: a small amount accumulates through the product. The latent period is up to several months, without signs. The predominant signs are encephalopathy and ataxia. Stomatitis and marked kidney damage are not expected.

The second teaching case: acute poisoning. This is a hypothetical case, not a real examination. Given: in the first hour a metallic taste and burning in the mouth, severe abdominal pain and incessant vomiting. Then cholera-like diarrhoea and cramps in the calves, the voice hoarse, and death on the second day. Questions: which form and which substance fit, what is expected in the body, which samples are examined?

The answer to the second case: the signs correspond to the gastrointestinal form of arsenic. The signs are cholera-like diarrhoea and cramps in the calves. In the body, thickened blood and intestinal inflammation are expected. Exact confirmation is obtained from the history and toxicological examination. As samples, blood, urine, vomit and gastric lavage fluid are taken.

Conclusion: four substances are compared; diagnosis rests on the whole picture and toxicology. With inorganic mercury, stomatitis and the sublimate kidney predominate, with additional inflammation of the large intestine. With organic mercury, toxic encephalopathy, chronic course and latent period. With lead, damage to the nervous system and anaemia. With thallium, alopecia and polyneuropathy, with additional gastroenteritis and ataxia. With arsenic, gastrointestinal or paralytic form, with cumulation in hair and nails.

The review questions rest on the review questions of the textbook. On diagnosis: what is the basis and what material is taken? On mercury: list the morphological signs. On organic mercury: how does it differ from inorganic? On lead: what changes occur in the body? On arsenic: state the two forms, the post-mortem signs and cumulation.
